lead: Two matrices can describe the same linear map in different bases. They are called similar, and one is P⁻¹AP for an invertible change-of-basis matrix P. Similar matrices share eigenvalues, trace, determinant and rank. Diagonalization asks for the best basis: one in which the map becomes a diagonal matrix. That happens exactly when the matrix has enough independent eigenvectors. The idea powers vibration analysis, Markov chains, and solving systems by decoupling them. This chapter gives the test, the construction of P and D, and the multiplicity condition that decides when diagonalization is possible.
prereq: You need: characteristic polynomials and eigenvectors from 4.1, eigenvalue bookkeeping from 4.2, and change of basis from Unit 3.

sections.h3: Similar matrices: same map, different basis

blocks.text: Two n×n matrices A and B are similar if B = P⁻¹AP for some invertible matrix P. The matrix P is a change-of-basis matrix: it rewrites vectors in a new basis. In that new basis, the same linear map has matrix B. Similarity is an equivalence relation: reflexive, symmetric and transitive.

blocks.where: A and B are n×n matrices over the same field; P is invertible. B is the matrix of the same linear map as A in the basis formed by the columns of P.

blocks.text: Similar matrices have the same characteristic polynomial: det(B − λI) = det(P⁻¹(A − λI)P) = det(A − λI). The determinant of a product splits, and det(P⁻¹) det(P) = 1. So B and A have the same eigenvalues with the same algebraic multiplicities.

items: The trace is unchanged: tr(B) = tr(P⁻¹AP) = tr(AP P⁻¹) = tr(A).
The determinant is unchanged: det(B) = det(P⁻¹) det(A) det(P) = det(A).
The rank and nullity are unchanged, because P and P⁻¹ are invertible.
The geometric multiplicity of each eigenvalue is unchanged.

blocks.text: The converse is false: two matrices with the same eigenvalues need not be similar. For example, [[1,0],[0,1]] and [[1,1],[0,1]] both have eigenvalue 1 twice, but only the first is diagonal.

A matrix A is diagonalizable if there exists an invertible P and a diagonal D such that P⁻¹AP = D. Equivalently A = PDP⁻¹. The diagonal entries of D are the eigenvalues of A, and the columns of P are matching eigenvectors.
Theorem. An n×n matrix A is diagonalizable if and only if it has n linearly independent eigenvectors.

Proof in one direction: if A = PDP⁻¹ with D = diag(λ₁,…,λₙ), then AP = PD. Column i of AP is A times column i of P. Column i of PD is λᵢ times column i of P. So each column of P is an eigenvector. Since P is invertible, its columns are independent.
Other direction: if v₁,…,vₙ are independent eigenvectors with A vᵢ = λᵢ vᵢ, put P = [v₁ … vₙ] and D = diag(λ₁,…,λₙ). Then AP = PD, so P⁻¹AP = D.
The order rule: column i of P must be an eigenvector for the eigenvalue in position i of D. Swapping eigenvectors without swapping eigenvalues gives the wrong product.

Multiplicity condition. For every eigenvalue λ, algebraic multiplicity = geometric multiplicity. The algebraic multiplicity is its multiplicity as a root of the characteristic polynomial. The geometric multiplicity is dim N(A − λI) = n − rank(A − λI). The total of the geometric multiplicities must reach n.

Distinct eigenvalues are sufficient but not necessary. If all n eigenvalues are distinct, their eigenvectors are automatically independent, so A is diagonalizable. If an eigenvalue repeats, diagonalization may still work when its eigenspace is large enough. Some syllabi call the distinct-eigenvalue case regular eigenvalues.
A matrix is defective if some eigenvalue has geometric multiplicity strictly less than its algebraic multiplicity. A defective matrix is not diagonalizable.

Example: A = [[1,1],[0,1]]. Its characteristic polynomial is (1−λ)², so λ = 1 has algebraic multiplicity 2. The matrix A − I = [[0,1],[0,0]] has rank 1, so its nullity is 2 − 1 = 1. The geometric multiplicity is 1. There is only one independent eigenvector, for example (1,0). We cannot build a 2×2 invertible P from eigenvectors.
This A is a shear. No change of basis turns a shear into a diagonal map, because a diagonal map scales both basis directions independently and cannot mix them.
Repeated eigenvalues do not always cause failure. A = [[2,0],[0,2]] has λ = 2 with algebraic multiplicity 2, and A − 2I = 0 has nullity 2, so it is already diagonal.

figure.caption: The test: find n independent eigenvectors; if they exist, put them as columns of P and the matching eigenvalues on the diagonal of D. If not, the matrix is defective and cannot be diagonalized.

spec.title: Diagonalization test
spec.aria: The test asks for n independent eigenvectors; if yes, form P and diagonal D, if no, the matrix is not diagonalizable.

examples.question: Diagonalize A = [[4, 1], [2, 3]] by finding an invertible P and a diagonal D with P⁻¹AP = D.
steps: Compute the characteristic polynomial: det(A − λI) = det([[4 − λ, 1], [2, 3 − λ]]) = (4 − λ)(3 − λ) − 2 = λ² − 7λ + 10.
Solve λ² − 7λ + 10 = 0: (λ − 5)(λ − 2) = 0, so λ₁ = 5 and λ₂ = 2.
For λ₁ = 5: A − 5I = [[−1, 1], [2, −2]]. The equation (A − 5I)v = 0 gives −x₁ + x₂ = 0, so x₂ = x₁. Choose v₁ = (1, 1).
For λ₂ = 2: A − 2I = [[2, 1], [2, 1]]. The equation gives 2x₁ + x₂ = 0, so x₂ = −2x₁. Choose v₂ = (1, −2).
Check independence: det P = det([[1, 1], [1, −2]]) = 1(−2) − 1(1) = −3 ≠ 0. The eigenvectors are independent.
Form P with v₁, v₂ as columns and D with matching eigenvalues: P = [[1, 1], [1, −2]], D = [[5, 0], [0, 2]].
examples.check:
A = [[4, 1], [2, 3]]
tr = A[0][0] + A[1][1]
detA = A[0][0]*A[1][1] - A[0][1]*A[1][0]
disc = tr*tr - 4*detA
l1 = (tr + disc**0.5)/2
l2 = (tr - disc**0.5)/2
print(int(round(l1)))
print(int(round(l2)))
P = [[1, 1], [1, -2]]
detP = P[0][0]*P[1][1] - P[0][1]*P[1][0]
Pinv = [[P[1][1]/detP, -P[0][1]/detP], [-P[1][0]/detP, P[0][0]/detP]]
def mul(X, Y):
    return [[sum(X[i][k]*Y[k][j] for k in range(2)) for j in range(2)] for i in range(2)]
D = mul(mul(Pinv, A), P)
assert abs(D[0][0] - l1) < 1e-9
assert abs(D[1][1] - l2) < 1e-9
assert abs(D[0][1]) < 1e-9 and abs(D[1][0]) < 1e-9

traps: Order mismatch: column i of P must pair with diagonal entry i of D.
A repeated eigenvalue is not automatic failure; check the geometric multiplicity.
Do not confuse algebraic multiplicity (root count) with geometric multiplicity (eigenspace dimension).
A diagonalizable matrix need not have distinct eigenvalues; the identity matrix is the simplest counterexample.
P must be invertible: independent eigenvectors are required, not just any list of eigenvectors.

quiz.a: A and B are similar if B = P⁻¹AP for some invertible matrix P.

quiz.q: State the diagonalization test in terms of eigenvectors.
quiz.a: An n×n matrix is diagonalizable if and only if it has n linearly independent eigenvectors.

quiz.q: Why do similar matrices have the same characteristic polynomial?
quiz.a: det(B − λI) = det(P⁻¹(A − λI)P) = det(P⁻¹) det(A − λI) det(P) = det(A − λI).

quiz.q: What does geometric multiplicity mean, and how is it computed?
quiz.a: It is dim N(A − λI) = n − rank(A − λI), the number of independent eigenvectors for λ.

quiz.q: For A = [[2,0],[1,2]], find the eigenvalues and decide whether A is diagonalizable.
quiz.a: Characteristic polynomial (2 − λ)², so λ = 2 twice. A − 2I = [[0,0],[1,0]] has rank 1 and nullity 1. Geometric multiplicity 1 < algebraic multiplicity 2, so A is not diagonalizable.

quiz.q: For A = [[4,1],[2,3]], write P and D with P⁻¹AP = D.
quiz.a: Eigenvalues 5 and 2. Eigenvectors (1,1) and (1,−2). P = [[1,1],[1,−2]], D = diag(5,2).

quiz.q: If an n×n matrix has n distinct eigenvalues, prove it is diagonalizable.
quiz.a: Eigenvectors from distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent. These n independent eigenvectors form the invertible matrix P. Then P⁻¹AP = D, where D holds the eigenvalues.

quiz.q: A 3×3 matrix has eigenvalues 1, 1, 2. Its eigenspace for λ = 1 has dimension 1. Is it diagonalizable? Explain.
quiz.a: No. The algebraic multiplicity of 1 is 2 but its geometric multiplicity is 1. The total independent eigenvectors is at most 1 + 1 = 2, less than 3.

beyond: Not for the exam. Similarity and diagonalization lead to the Jordan canonical form, which handles defective matrices by allowing 1s above the diagonal. In numerical work, eigenvalues are computed by iterative algorithms such as QR, not by solving the characteristic polynomial exactly. Diagonalization decouples coupled differential equations and powers Aᵏ; Markov chains use it to find long-run behaviour. Search next for Jordan form, matrix exponential and eigendecomposition stability.
